content: 1. Develop and implement a comprehensive communication plan, including biosafety measures, to minimize exposure to avian influenza among at-risk populations. 2. In affected areas, the public should avoid contact with chickens, ducks, or other birds and stay away from locations where poultry is housed, slaughtered, or prepared. 3. Children should not handle birds, their waste (including feathers and manure), collect eggs, or assist in slaughtering or food preparation involving poultry. 4. Ensure poultry and poultry products are thoroughly cooked before consumption. 5. If handling birds or bird feces in affected areas, wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), such as gloves and boots, and wash hands, shoes, and clothing immediately afterward. 6. Individuals working in live bird markets or involved in slaughtering and processing birds should wear light-colored protective clothing, clean aprons, gloves, and rubber boots. If these are unavailable, plastic bags can be used to cover hands and feet. 7. Wash hands with soap and water immediately after handling birds or their by-products if gloves are not used. 8. Seek medical attention promptly if feeling unwell and report any sick or unexpectedly dead poultry to authorities. 9. Do not slaughter or consume birds showing signs of illness or those that have died unexpectedly. 10. Provide appropriate PPE and training for professionals exposed to potentially infected birds or contaminated environments. 11. Maintain records of exposed professionals and monitor their health for seven days post-exposure. 12. Promote thorough cooking of poultry and poultry products to ensure food safety. 13. Separate raw meat from cooked or ready-to-eat foods to prevent cross-contamination. 14. Wash hands, surfaces, and utensils thoroughly after handling raw poultry or eggs. 15. Cook all poultry products, including eggs, thoroughly. Egg yolks should not be runny, and poultry meat should reach an internal temperature of 70°C (158°F). 16. Handle and store meat properly to avoid exposure to the virus during slaughter or post-slaughter processes. 17. Improve hygiene and biosecurity in live poultry markets to reduce the risk of virus transmission. 18. Implement Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) systems to identify and mitigate risks in food production processes, specifically for avian influenza viruses. 19. Treat drinking water from open reservoirs carefully to minimize risks, and advise the public to boil or chlorinate water if community treatment systems are unavailable. 20. Reduce contact with animal feces, as infected birds can shed large amounts of the virus in their waste. 21. Bury dead infected animals and contaminated solid waste at least one to two meters above groundwater or consider composting with restricted access to scavenging animals. 22. Investigate suspected human cases of avian influenza promptly to provide appropriate treatment, identify potential human contacts, and monitor for human-to-human transmission. 23. Enhance surveillance and awareness of human cases of avian influenza, including active and passive approaches in healthcare and community settings. 24. Monitor individuals exposed to avian influenza for the duration of the exposure period plus an additional seven days, with daily temperature checks and reporting of any health issues. 25. Collect diagnostic specimens from suspected human cases safely and ensure proper packaging, transport, and testing at qualified laboratories. 26. Share virus isolates with WHO Collaborating Centers to study virus evolution and adapt diagnostics and vaccines accordingly. 27. Prepare healthcare facilities to manage avian influenza cases, including implementing infection control measures to prevent nosocomial spread, raising awareness among healthcare workers, and establishing screening and triaging systems.
